```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(mediaPlanSim)
```

## Purpose and scope

A model of the distribution of contacts of a media plan receives, in practice,
the reach of one and of two insertions of each vehicle and the duplication
between vehicles, and returns the probability of each number of contacts. To
check such a model one needs a population in which the whole distribution of
contacts is known. Survey data rarely provide it, because they record at most a
declared frequency or the exposure of a single day.

`mediaPlanSim` builds such populations from explicit mechanisms. Given the
propensity of a person to be exposed to each vehicle, the contacts with vehicle
$j$ are binomial with $n_j$ trials and that propensity, and vehicles are
independent given the propensities. The mechanisms differ only in how the
propensities are generated and linked.

Three limits must be kept in mind:

* Data simulated from a mechanism inherit its assumptions. Reproducing the truth
  of a mechanism does not show that a model describes real audiences.
* Insertions of the same vehicle are exchangeable given the propensity. This
  excludes, for example, a person whose exposure depends on the order or timing
  of insertions.
* Only vehicles with a bounded number of insertions are generated.
  Vehicles with an unbounded stream of impressions are not covered.

## Scenarios

```{r scenarios}
r1 <- c(TV = 0.20, Press = 0.15, Radio = 0.12)
r2 <- c(0.312, 0.239, 0.195)
n  <- c(5, 4, 6)

indep <- scenario_independent(r1, r2, n)
gauss <- scenario_gaussian(r1, r2, n, rho = 0.4)
indep
```

A latent-class scenario describes an audience made of segments. Segments that
follow different vehicles generate duplication below what independence implies.

```{r latent}
segments <- scenario_latent_class(
  class_prob = c(0.35, 0.35, 0.30),
  class_propensity = cbind(A = c(0.45, 0.15, 0.15), B = c(0.15, 0.45, 0.15)),
  insertions = c(4, 4)
)
pm <- population_moments(segments)
pm$dup
prod(pm$r1)  # duplication under independence, for comparison
```

## The truth and the inputs of a model

`exposure_truth()` returns the true distribution of contacts of the plan, and
`population_moments()` the reach of one and two insertions and the duplication,
which are the inputs a model would receive.

```{r truth}
tr <- exposure_truth(gauss)
tr$metrics[c("grp", "reach_1plus", "reach_3plus", "ots")]
round(tr$moments$dup, 4)
```

For independent and latent-class scenarios the truth is exact. For the Gaussian
copula it is computed by deterministic quasi-Monte Carlo integration, so the
`n_qmc` argument controls its accuracy; two values can be compared to judge it.

```{r qmc}
distribution_error(exposure_truth(gauss, 8192), exposure_truth(gauss, 65536))
```

## Simulated respondents

```{r simulate}
sim <- simulate_exposure(gauss, N = 20000, seed = 2026)
sim
head(as.data.frame(sim), 3)
```

The estimated moments approach the population moments as `N` grows, and the
empirical distribution approaches the truth.

```{r sample}
round(sample_moments(sim)$r1 - population_moments(gauss)$r1, 4)
distribution_error(empirical_distribution(sim), tr)
```

## Scoring a model: dependence matters

The simplest model ignores dependence and takes the convolution of the
Beta-Binomial marginals. Its error against the truth depends on the mechanism.

```{r indep-model}
indep_model <- exposure_truth(indep)   # the independence model for this plan
scenarios <- list(
  "rho = -0.3" = scenario_gaussian(r1, r2, n, rho = -0.3),
  "rho = 0"    = scenario_gaussian(r1, r2, n, rho = 0),
  "rho = 0.4"  = scenario_gaussian(r1, r2, n, rho = 0.4),
  "rho = 0.8"  = scenario_gaussian(r1, r2, n, rho = 0.8)
)
errs <- t(sapply(scenarios, function(s) {
  distribution_error(indep_model, exposure_truth(s))[c("tv", "reach_1plus")]
}))
round(errs, 4)
```

The row for `rho = 0` shows the numerical error of the quasi-Monte Carlo truth, since
there the independence model is exact.

## The same moments do not fix the distribution

Two mechanisms can share the reach of one and two insertions of every vehicle
and the duplication between vehicles, and still differ in the distribution of
contacts. The next chunk calibrates the correlation of a Gaussian copula so that
it reproduces the duplication of a latent-class mechanism.

```{r identification}
lc <- scenario_latent_class(
  class_prob = c(0.35, 0.35, 0.30),
  class_propensity = cbind(A = c(0.45, 0.15, 0.15), B = c(0.15, 0.45, 0.15)),
  insertions = c(4, 4)
)
pm <- population_moments(lc)
gap <- function(rho) {
  population_moments(scenario_gaussian(pm$r1, pm$r2, c(4, 4), rho))$dup[1, 2] -
    pm$dup[1, 2]
}
rho <- uniroot(gap, c(-0.99, 0))$root
gc <- scenario_gaussian(pm$r1, pm$r2, c(4, 4), rho)

mom <- function(s) {
  m <- population_moments(s)
  c(r1_A = unname(m$r1[1]), r1_B = unname(m$r1[2]),
    r2_A = unname(m$r2[1]), r2_B = unname(m$r2[2]), dup = m$dup[1, 2])
}
round(rbind(latent_class = mom(lc), gaussian = mom(gc)), 4)
round(distribution_error(exposure_truth(gc), exposure_truth(lc)), 4)
```

Moments of this kind therefore leave part of the distribution undetermined, and
a model that outperforms another in one mechanism may not do so in another.
Benchmarks should state the mechanisms they use and should include several.

## Matching the dependence of real data

A scenario is only as useful as its resemblance to the data it stands for. When a
survey gives the reach of one insertion and the duplication between vehicles,
`calibrate_gaussian()` builds a Gaussian-copula scenario that reproduces them,
and `compare_to_observed()` checks, against sampling noise, whether the
distribution of contacts of the scenario is compatible with the observed one.

The next chunk uses a known mechanism as a stand-in for a survey, so that the
outcome can be judged. Half of the respondents calibrate the scenario and the
other half test it, which avoids judging a calibration with the data it was
fitted to.

```{r calibrate}
r1 <- c(A = 0.14, B = 0.05, C = 0.02)
r2 <- r1 + 0.4 * (r1 - r1^2)
truth <- scenario_gaussian(r1, r2, c(1, 1, 1),
                           matrix(c(1, .6, .3, .6, 1, .5, .3, .5, 1), 3))
survey <- simulate_exposure(truth, N = 20000, seed = 10)$contacts
fit_half <- survey[1:10000, ]
test_half <- survey[10001:20000, ]

m <- colMeans(fit_half)
dup <- crossprod(fit_half) / nrow(fit_half)
scn <- calibrate_gaussian(m, NULL, c(1, 1, 1), dup)
round(attr(scn, "calibration")$rho, 2)

ind <- scenario_independent(m, m + 0.5 * (m - m^2), c(1, 1, 1))
sapply(list(calibrated = scn, independent = ind), function(s) {
  unlist(compare_to_observed(s, test_half, B = 100, seed = 1)[
    c("tv_observed", "tv_bootstrap_mean", "p_value")])
})
```

A small `tv_observed` that does not exceed the bootstrap distance, together with a
large `p_value`, indicates that the scenario is compatible with the held-out
respondents; the independent scenario is not.

Three cautions apply to real data. First, a Gaussian copula with Beta marginals
cannot reproduce every duplication: `attr(scn, "calibration")$flagged` lists the
pairs that stay out of reach, and `r2 = "auto"` makes the propensities more
dispersed, which is an assumption and not an observation. Second, a free
correlation for every pair adapts to the noise of the sample, above all for rare
vehicles; `n_eff`, `shrink` and `rank` regularise it, but regularising is not
free, and the held-out comparison is the way to decide whether it pays. Third, a survey of one day of reading, for example,
cannot show how the vehicles behave over several insertions, so a scenario
calibrated on it describes what it observed, and nothing more.

## Plans, microdata and files

One calibrated universe of vehicles serves many plans: `scenario_subset()`
extracts the vehicles of a plan and sets their insertions. Contacts per vehicle
are the default output; `insertion_level = TRUE` returns one 0/1 column per
insertion. Both can be written to CSV or Excel.

```{r export-files}
plan <- scenario_subset(scn, c("A", "C"), insertions = c(4, 2))
sim <- simulate_exposure(plan, N = 1000, seed = 3, insertion_level = TRUE)
head(as.data.frame(sim, level = "insertion"), 3)
f <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
export_microdata(sim, f, level = "insertion")
dim(read.csv(f))
```

## Use with other software

The package depends only on base R and `stats`. To feed a model implemented
elsewhere, export the moments or the respondents:

```{r export, eval = FALSE}
pm <- population_moments(gauss)      # r1, r2, dup, insertions
write.csv(as.data.frame(sim), "respondents.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

and read the file from another environment, for example with
`pandas.read_csv("respondents.csv")` in Python. The columns are `id`, one column
of contacts per vehicle, and `total`.
